title: Design and construct complex eukaryotic genomes to specification

concept.text: The innovation would be a reliable way to design and build substantially redesigned eukaryotic genomes whose intended functions survive construction and operate in living cells. A usable workflow would connect specification, DNA synthesis, assembly, introduction into cells, verification and debugging across multiple chromosomes. Success would require the resulting organisms to meet stated functional requirements, including growth, chromosome inheritance and regulatory behavior.

The defining advance is dependable coordination across an entire genome: chromosome organization, gene regulation and interactions among many changes would have to remain compatible. Existing synthetic yeast chromosome work provides concrete foundations, but individual chromosome construction and partial consolidation do not establish this broader capability. Extending the approach across species would also require accommodating differences in chromatin, epigenetic regulation, transcription and cellular pathways.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make whole eukaryotic genomes a practical medium for controlled experiments. Researchers could construct alternative chromosome organizations, redistribute genetic functions, compare regulatory architectures and test interacting genetic circuits against explicit predictions. Existing chromosome rearrangement methods and modular synthetic platforms provide a technical basis for this inference; reliable construction would make such comparisons more systematic and repeatable.

A direct consequence would be greater experimental control over how large genetic systems are organized. Useful biomanufacturing organisms could follow, including strains engineered to produce proteins or metabolites, but those applications remain conditional. Building a specified sequence and maintaining its function would not automatically reveal which design produces a desirable organism-level trait. Predicting performance across genetic backgrounds and environments remains an additional challenge, and successful yeast engineering would not establish equivalent control over all complex eukaryotes.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an integrated, reproducible design-to-organism process that can deliver functional, substantially redesigned multi-chromosome genomes without relying on extensive unexplained corrections after construction. Physical assembly remains a substantial barrier: the synXVI work identified tandem duplications of assembled DNA segments, deletions, vector insertions, missing intended codon substitutions and retained native introns. These errors show why assembling a chromosome must be followed by sequence verification and repair.

Correct sequence assembly also leaves biological design problems. Repetitive DNA complicates construction; regulatory insertions and removal of tRNA genes can affect fitness; and changes that work individually can become problematic when synthetic chromosomes are combined. Chromosome segregation and stable inheritance must remain reliable as genome organization changes. The engineering challenge therefore includes identifying which defects arise from construction errors, which arise from the intended design and which emerge through interactions among changes.

Broader applicability would require designs that respect species-specific chromatin organization, epigenetic regulation, transcriptional machinery and pathway connectivity. Long-range regulation is a relevant design constraint at this broader level; the supplied evidence does not establish it as a particular mechanism demonstrated by the synXVI experiments. The review discusses these issues as constraints on cross-species chromosome platforms, rather than demonstrating that they have been solved.

current_state.text: Goold, Kroukamp, Erpf and colleagues published Construction and iterative redesign of synXVI a 903 kb synthetic Saccharomyces cerevisiae chromosome on 20 January 2025, DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-55318-3. They report assembly and debugging of a 902,994-base-pair synthetic yeast chromosome within the Sc2.0 project. The project’s stated genome construction goal comprises 16 synthetic chromosomes and an additional tRNA neochromosome. The paper’s subsequent chromosome redesign was computational: that later redesign should not be counted as a separately constructed and experimentally validated chromosome.

Archer, Walker, Erpf, Paulsen and Pretorius published the review One Yeast, Sixteen Synthetic Chromosomes, Infinite Possibilities on 19 May 2026, DOI 10.1002/yea.70026. It reports that functional synthetic versions of all 16 native yeast chromosomes have been delivered. This describes achievements across the chromosome set; it does not mean that all 16 had been consolidated into one cell.

Section 4.2 of that review identifies full consolidation as a remaining challenge and describes six complete synthetic chromosomes plus one synthetic chromosome arm combined in one strain, representing approximately one-third of the haploid S. cerevisiae genome. The review attributes that consolidation result to a 2023 study, so it should not be presented as a new experiment performed in 2026. These achievements demonstrate chromosome construction, debugging and partial genome consolidation in yeast, while falling short of the proposed reproducible, predictive platform spanning multiple species.

The supplied evidence review assessed the synXVI article’s full main text, methods and references, and the 2026 review’s complete main text and references through an alternative full-text XML copy. It did not inspect the synXVI supplementary files or figure images, or the review’s figure images; the conclusions above do not depend on those unavailable visual inspections. The review’s author metadata was verified in the supplied assessment, resolving the earlier uncertainty about authorship. No freshness search record was supplied, so these dated sources do not establish the latest state through 1 November 2026 or exclude subsequent progress.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent laboratories would construct several substantially redesigned multi-chromosome genomes in at least two eukaryotic species, starting from explicit sequence and functional specifications. The resulting organisms would exhibit pre-specified growth, inheritance and regulatory behaviors across generations. Independent verification would establish genome integrity, and investigators would document any rescue mutations and their functional roles. Extensive unexplained rescue changes would weaken the claim that performance follows reliably from the specified design.
completion_criteria.label: Redesigned genomes meet functional specifications across laboratories and two species

completion_criteria.text: Proposed operational requirements: before testing, investigators would define how many genomes constitute several, what qualifies as substantial redesign, the generation counts and environments to be examined, acceptable deviations from intended behavior and permissible rescue changes. Reproduction across laboratories should include the construction and debugging process, as well as measurements of the finished organisms. Reporting construction failures, repair effort and unsuccessful designs would help establish the practical boundaries of the workflow.
completion_criteria.label: Construction and debugging reproduce across laboratories under predefined acceptance criteria

completion_criteria.text: The rationale for testing beyond simple viability comes from observed construction defects, consolidation-related fitness problems and the review’s emphasis on evaluating synthetic yeast under both basal and challenging conditions. The exact thresholds proposed here are not published standards. A successful two-species program would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested designs, environments and generations; it would not prove universal applicability across eukaryotes or unrestricted prediction of organism-level traits.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated breadth remains limited to tested designs, environments and generations

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: GEN-01, A predictive, causal map of the genome’s regulatory code, and GEN-11, Predicting genetic interactions across backgrounds and environments, would supply complementary design knowledge. GEN-01 concerns predicting regulatory consequences; GEN-11 concerns the combined effects of genetic changes under different conditions. GEN-02 concerns constructing and validating the resulting genomes. Genome construction could test both kinds of prediction, but successful construction alone would not solve either predictive problem.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-03, Precise, programmable replacement of large genomic regions in existing cells, overlaps with the introduction and repair steps needed for genome construction. Its central objective is reliable replacement within an existing genome, whereas GEN-02 requires coordinated function across a substantially redesigned multi-chromosome genome. GEN-04, A retargetable delivery platform for genetic medicines across the body, shares the challenge of delivering genetic material into cells, but adds tissue targeting and organism-wide therapeutic delivery requirements that are distinct from constructing synthetic genomes in experimental organisms.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-05, General laws of environmentally induced, sequence-independent inheritance, addresses inherited effects that need not be encoded by changes in DNA sequence. Such effects could influence whether a constructed genome behaves consistently across generations. GEN-02 must account for relevant epigenetic context when validating a design, but building a genome would not establish general laws of environmentally induced inheritance.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-06, Transferable clonal seed reproduction across major crops, and GEN-07, Predictably controllable inheritance in wild populations, both concern control over inheritance in particular biological settings. Genome construction might eventually support designs used in those settings, but it would not itself establish clonal seed reproduction or predictable population-level spread. GEN-02’s requirement for stable chromosome inheritance in constructed organisms remains distinct from those reproductive and ecological capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-08, Reconstructing an organism’s cell divisions and histories from inherited molecular marks, concerns reading developmental history. Constructed genomes could potentially incorporate recording systems, while lineage measurements could help evaluate developmental behavior. The overlap is enabling and experimental: reconstructing cell history and constructing a functional genome remain separate achievements.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-09, An autonomous, evolvable expanded genetic alphabet, would change the molecular information system available to living organisms. GEN-02 could pursue extensive genome redesign using the existing alphabet and does not require its expansion. GEN-10, A testable reconstruction of the origin and fixation of the genetic code, concerns a historical explanatory problem. Synthetic genomes could provide experimental systems for testing aspects of code organization, but constructing them would not by itself reconstruct the code’s origin or fixation.

change_log.change: Expanded the concept into an integrated workflow covering specification, synthesis, assembly, introduction, verification, debugging and inherited function.
change_log.reason: Preserves the research’s full engineering scope and the review’s distinction between sequence construction and functional genome design.

change_log.change: Distinguished experimentally constructed and debugged 902,994-base-pair synXVI from the paper’s subsequent computational redesign.
change_log.reason: Prevents an in silico result from being presented as an additional physical construction.

change_log.change: Replaced the obsolete review-author verification caveat with the verified authors Archer, Walker, Erpf, Paulsen and Pretorius.
change_log.reason: The supplied assessment verified that metadata from the retained full-text artifact.

change_log.change: Separated functional synthetic versions of all 16 native yeast chromosomes from their consolidation into a single cell, and dated the cited six-chromosome-plus-one-arm result to 2023.
change_log.reason: The 2026 review reports earlier consolidation work and does not establish a fully consolidated synthetic genome.

change_log.change: Integrated specific assembly errors, regulatory and tRNA-related fitness effects, consolidation problems, segregation requirements and cross-species constraints.
change_log.reason: These details explain why individual chromosome achievements do not yet establish a broadly usable genome construction platform.

change_log.change: Qualified long-range regulation as a broader chromatin and epigenetic design consideration.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports that broader constraint without identifying it as a specific mechanism demonstrated in the synXVI experiments.

change_log.change: Preserved conditional experimental and biomanufacturing significance while distinguishing construction from organism-level trait prediction.
change_log.reason: The sources motivate those possibilities without demonstrating general predictive control over useful traits.

change_log.change: Made completion criteria explicitly proposed, retained independent laboratories and two species, and added operational definitions and bounded interpretation.
change_log.reason: The criteria are evaluation proposals rather than established standards, and finite demonstrations cannot establish universal applicability.

change_log.change: Added distinctions covering every other supplied roster entry and preserved evidence-access and freshness limitations.
change_log.reason: The record must stand alone without merging related concepts or implying broader document inspection or a current-state search.

unresolved_issues: Subsequent progress through 1 November 2026 remains unassessed because the supplied freshness search record is empty; source retrieval dates do not resolve that gap.

The proposed demonstration still requires numerical definitions for genome count, redesign extent, generation counts, environmental coverage, acceptable functional deviations and permissible rescue changes.
The species and redesign classes needed to establish useful breadth beyond yeast remain unspecified; two species alone would not establish applicability throughout complex eukaryotes.
The supplied assessment did not inspect supplementary files or figure images for synXVI, or figure images for the 2026 review. Claims requiring those materials cannot be resolved from this record.
